What the official sources say

  • An action to recover land from a person in peaceable and adverse possession, cultivating, using and enjoying it, must be commenced within ten years after the cause of action accrues; the possession covers no more than 160 acres (or the enclosed acreage if less), unless held under a recorded written memorandum of title fixing boundaries. (A.R.S. 12-526; source)
  • An action to recover real property from a person in peaceable and adverse possession under title or color of title must be commenced within three years; 'color of title' means a consecutive chain of transfer down to the possessor that is irregular (for example an unrecorded or only written link) but without want of intrinsic fairness and honesty. (A.R.S. 12-523; source)
  • A person is guilty of forcible entry and detainer if he enters real property except where entry is given by law, enters by force, or wilfully and without force holds over after the term ends and after demand for possession by the person entitled. (A.R.S. 12-1171; source)

Arizona Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Arizona house?

Check the statute and talk to a Arizona attorney about your facts.

How long does adverse possession take in Arizona?

Under A.R.S. 12-526, a person who has peaceable and adverse possession of land, and is cultivating, using and enjoying it, is protected once the owner waits ten years after the cause of action accrues. The owner who wants the land back has to start a lawsuit within those ten years and not afterward.

The statute puts a cap on the claim. The possession cannot cover more than 160 acres, including improvements, or the number of acres actually enclosed if that is less. When possession is taken under a recorded written memorandum of title other than a deed that fixes the boundaries, the claim reaches as far as the boundaries stated in that paper.

For a homeowner, the lesson is simple. A person who moves into a vacant house has not acquired title the next week. The ten-year clock in 12-526 is about slow, open and uncontested use, and an owner who acts early keeps full control of the property.

Is a squatter the same as a tenant in Arizona?

No. A tenant has an agreement with the owner, and a squatter does not. The difference decides which process an owner uses to get the person out.

Arizona's forcible detainer law reaches people other than tenants. Under A.R.S. 12-1173.01, a person who keeps possession after written demand may be removed through an action for forcible detainer filed with the clerk of the superior court if the property:

  • was sold through foreclosure of a mortgage, deed of trust or contract for conveyance,
  • was sold through a trustee's sale under a deed of trust,
  • was forfeited through a contract for conveyance,
  • was sold by virtue of an execution and the title has been duly transferred, or
  • was sold by the owner and the title has been duly transferred.

The same statute protects people with a lease or other possessory right that is superior to the interest sold. It also says these remedies add to other remedies and do not replace them.

How fast is an Arizona eviction case against someone with no right to stay?

Arizona's forcible detainer process is built to move quickly. After a complaint is filed in writing and under oath with the superior court clerk or a justice of the peace, A.R.S. 12-1175 says summons must issue no later than the next judicial day, and it must be served at least two days before the return date.

The complaint has to describe the premises well enough to identify them and has to state the facts that entitle the plaintiff to possession. The statute also bars state agencies and individual courts from requiring a mandatory form for notices or pleadings, as long as the document meets the statutory content rules.

Under A.R.S. 12-1176, a plaintiff's jury request must be granted, and the trial date is no more than five judicial days after the complaint is filed. A superior court jury has eight members and a justice court jury has six. If the plaintiff does not ask for a jury, the defendant can.

What happens after the judge rules for the owner?

If the court finds the defendant guilty of forcible detainer, it gives the plaintiff judgment for restitution of the premises, and it grants a writ of restitution. A.R.S. 12-1178 also lets the court award damages, attorney fees and costs, plus unpaid rent if the case involves a rental agreement.

StepWhat the statute says
Judgment for plaintiffRestitution of the premises, damages, fees and costs, and a writ of restitution
Waiting periodNo writ issues until five calendar days after judgment
Motion to set asideDoes not stop the writ unless a judge finds good cause
Judgment for defendantDefendant gets damages, fees and costs, and a writ if the plaintiff took possession in the meantime
Staying after service of writCriminal trespass in the third degree under 13-1502 for a dwelling unit, mobile home space or RV space

The court must give a defendant who loses notice of that criminal trespass rule.

Is entering a vacant house in Arizona a crime?

It can be. A.R.S. 13-1504 defines criminal trespass in the first degree as knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully in a residential structure or in a fenced residential yard, among other conduct. Entering or remaining unlawfully in a residential structure is a class 6 felony. Doing so in a fenced residential yard is a class 1 misdemeanor.

The same statute covers entering a residential yard and looking into the home in reckless disregard of the occupant's privacy, which is also a class 1 misdemeanor. Criminal trespass is a matter for law enforcement. If you find someone living in a house you own, ask the police how they handle it and ask an attorney whether to file a civil case at the same time.

Do not change locks, shut off utilities or remove belongings from an occupied home without legal advice. The statutes above give owners court tools, and the court process is how an owner gets a lawful result.

How should an Arizona owner protect a vacant house from squatters?

The best protection is attention, and the statutes show why. Because the adverse possession period is ten years and an owner can sue to recover land at any time before that, the practical task is to notice a problem early and act on it.

  • Visit the house on a schedule and keep a log with dates and photos.
  • Keep the tax bill, the insurance and the utilities current in the owner's name or the estate's name.
  • Secure doors, windows and gates, and post clear no-trespassing signs.
  • Give neighbors a phone number to call if they see activity.
  • If someone is inside, get the police report number and talk to an attorney about written demand and a forcible detainer complaint.

Vacant houses are often inherited homes, rentals after a tenant leaves, or properties in probate. They are also the houses we are asked to buy. If the cost and delay of managing an occupied or neglected house are wearing you down, a cash sale as-is is one way out.

Can you sell an Arizona house with a squatter inside?

Yes, a sale is possible, though the occupant affects the price, the timing and the title company's comfort. A buyer who is paying cash can accept an occupied property as-is, and the price reflects that. Any closing still depends on the title company confirming who can sign and what is recorded against the property.

Tell us what you know: how long the person has been there, whether anyone has given permission, whether you have served a written demand and whether a case is filed. We buy houses across Arizona in any condition and will explain what we can and cannot do with the facts you give us.

What did we leave out of this Arizona squatter guide?

We did not confirm the notice periods for different kinds of occupants, the color-of-title statute beyond what is already on this page, or any recent changes to how counties handle unlawful occupants. Those points depend on the facts, so talk with an Arizona attorney or the court that would hear your case.

More questions about Arizona Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

How many years of adverse possession are required in Arizona?

Ten years of peaceable and adverse possession, with the owner losing the right to sue after that period under A.R.S. 12-526. The claim is limited to 160 acres or the enclosed acreage if smaller.

How fast is an Arizona forcible detainer trial?

The trial date is no more than five judicial days after the complaint is filed, according to A.R.S. 12-1176. The summons must issue by the next judicial day and be served at least two days before the return date.

How long until a writ of restitution is issued in Arizona?

Not until five calendar days after judgment. A motion to set aside the judgment does not delay the writ unless a judge finds good cause, under A.R.S. 12-1178.

Is staying in a house after a writ of restitution a crime in Arizona?

Yes. A defendant served with a writ who remains in or returns to the dwelling without the owner's permission commits criminal trespass in the third degree under A.R.S. 13-1502, as referenced in 12-1178.

Is unlawful entry into a residence a felony in Arizona?

Entering or remaining unlawfully in a residential structure is criminal trespass in the first degree and a class 6 felony under A.R.S. 13-1504. Doing it in a fenced residential yard is a class 1 misdemeanor.

What the official sources say

  • Security deposit plus prepaid rent may not exceed one and one-half month's rent (tenant may voluntarily prepay more). (A.R.S. 33-1321; source)

What must an Arizona landlord tell a tenant in writing?

At or before the start of a tenancy, an Arizona landlord must give the tenant in writing the name and address of the person who manages the premises and of an owner or agent who can accept legal papers and notices. The landlord must also state in writing that the Arizona residential landlord and tenant act is posted on the Arizona Department of Housing website.

This information has to stay current and be given again when the tenant asks. The duty extends to any successor landlord, owner or manager, which matters when a house changes hands. A landlord who skips these steps becomes an agent of every landlord for service of process and for receiving notices and demands.

When there is a written lease, the landlord must hand over a signed copy, the tenant must return one fully signed copy, and all blank spaces must be filled in. Leaving this undone counts as a material noncompliance by whichever side failed to do it.

When is rent due, and what kind of tenancy exists without a set term?

Unless the parties agreed otherwise, rent is due at the dwelling without any demand or notice, at the start of the period. Monthly rent is due at the start of each month, and rent is spread evenly day to day when a partial month is involved.

If there is no lease at all, the tenant owes the fair rental value for using the unit. If a lease does not fix a definite term, the tenancy is month to month, except that a roomer paying weekly rent has a week to week tenancy.

These default rules matter when a landlord inherits or buys a house with a tenant who has never signed anything. The tenant is still a tenant with statutory rights, and the seller or buyer should find out what the actual arrangement is before closing.

Which lease clauses are not allowed in Arizona?

A rental agreement cannot make a tenant give up the rights and remedies the act provides, and a clause that does is unenforceable. The statute names five kinds of prohibited promises.

  • Waiving or giving up rights or remedies under the landlord tenant chapter.
  • Paying the landlord's attorney fees, though a written lease may let the prevailing party in a court case recover fees.
  • Excusing the landlord from liability or agreeing to indemnify the landlord for it.
  • Giving up the right to call police or emergency help.
  • Paying a penalty because the tenant, or anyone else, called for emergency help.

A landlord who knowingly uses a lease with such terms can owe the tenant actual damages plus up to two months of periodic rent. A landlord who is also a seller should have an attorney read an old lease before handing it to a buyer, since a bad clause can create exposure.

How does an Arizona landlord end a tenancy for nonpayment or breach?

The notice period depends on the problem. For unpaid rent the landlord gives written notice and the tenant has five days to pay before the landlord may file a special detainer action. For most other material breaches the notice gives ten days to fix the problem. A serious health or safety breach by the tenant gets a five day notice. A material and irreparable breach, such as violence, certain drug activity or serious property damage, allows immediate termination notice.

Material falsification on the rental application, such as lying about occupants, pets, income or prior evictions, is also a breach, and falsification about criminal history or prior evictions cannot be cured.

SituationNotice period
Unpaid rentFive days after written notice
Material breach of the leaseTen days to cure
Breach affecting health and safetyFive days to cure
Material and irreparable breachImmediate termination notice

Notices sent by certified mail are treated as received on the actual delivery date or five days after mailing, whichever is first.

Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying?

Sometimes. Before a special detainer action is filed, the lease is reinstated if the tenant pays all past due rent and a reasonable late fee set out in the written lease. After filing, reinstatement requires the past due rent, late fees, attorney fees and court costs. Once the landlord has a judgment, reinstating the lease is up to the landlord.

A tenant may not hold back rent for any reason the act does not authorize. One authorized route is self help for minor defects. If the landlord fails to meet the habitability duties and the repair costs less than $300 or half of one month's rent, whichever is more, the tenant may give written notice, wait ten days, and then have a licensed contractor do the work and deduct the cost from rent after giving the landlord an itemized statement and a lien waiver. This is not allowed when the tenant or a guest caused the damage.

How fast is an Arizona special detainer case?

The process is quick by design. The summons is issued the day the complaint is filed, and the return date must be no fewer than three and no more than six days after the summons date. The summons must be served at least two days before the return day.

If personal service is attempted and fails, service can be completed by posting a copy of the summons on the front entrance within one day and mailing a copy by certified mail the same day, and the tenant is treated as served three days after mailing. A trial may be postponed for good cause supported by an affidavit, by up to three days in justice court or five days in superior court.

If the landlord wins, the court gives judgment for possession, stated late charges, costs, and at the landlord's option the unpaid rent. It then issues a writ of restitution. For a material and irreparable breach, the trial is set within three days of filing, and restitution is ordered at least twelve and no more than twenty four hours after a finding.

What happens to a tenant's belongings if the tenant dies or cannot be reached?

A landlord may ask a tenant to name a person who can enter the unit and retrieve belongings and any pet if the tenant dies or is incapacitated. If the landlord cannot reach that person, or the person does not answer within one day for an animal or ten days for other property after written contact, the landlord may dispose of the property under the abandoned property statute.

The authorized person must show government photo identification and has twenty days after first written contact, or after the last paid rent date if longer, to remove items and return the keys. Once the landlord lets the person in to remove belongings, the landlord has no further liability for those items. These rules for personal property apply when periodic rent has been unpaid for at least five days.

What should a landlord check before selling a rented Arizona house?

The best preparation is to know exactly what the lease and the statute require before a buyer asks. The deposit and entry rules summarized above are only part of the picture, and the points below fill in the gaps.

  • Confirm the written disclosure of manager and owner contact details was given and is current.
  • Gather the signed lease, any addenda, and records of rent paid and late fees charged.
  • Review the lease for prohibited clauses and fix the paperwork if needed.
  • Confirm whether the tenancy is month to month, since that sets the notice needed to end it.
  • Document any open repair requests, because unresolved habitability issues carry remedies for the tenant.

A buyer who takes the house as is will usually step into the landlord's position, including the deposit duties, so share the lease file early. A seller facing a tenant dispute should treat the notice rules above as firm and consult an attorney before serving any notice, because the statute spells out how notices must be delivered and what they must say.

More questions about Arizona Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

How many days does a tenant have to pay rent after notice in Arizona?

Five days. If the tenant does not pay within five days of the landlord's written notice of nonpayment, the landlord may file a special detainer action.

How long does an Arizona landlord wait for a tenant to fix a lease breach?

Ten days for most material breaches, and five days when the breach affects health and safety. A material and irreparable breach can lead to immediate termination notice.

Can an Arizona lease make a tenant pay the landlord's attorney fees?

Not as a one sided term. A written lease may let the prevailing party recover fees, but a clause making the tenant pay the landlord's fees alone is prohibited and unenforceable.

Is a notice sent by certified mail effective right away in Arizona?

No. It is treated as received on the day it actually arrives or five days after mailing, whichever happens first.

What is a special detainer action in Arizona?

It is the court case a landlord files to recover possession of a rental for nonpayment or breach. The summons issues the day of filing and the return date is set three to six days later.

Arizona Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Health-and-safety noncompliance by tenant (33-1341): five days' notice; material and irreparable breach on the premises (e.g., weapon discharge, controlled substances, assault, serious property damage): written notice for immediate termination under 33-1377. (A.R.S. 33-1368; source)
  • Special detainer: summons returnable not more than six nor less than three days from issuance; on judgment for plaintiff, court gives judgment for restitution of premises, late charges, costs and (at plaintiff's option) rent due, and grants a writ of restitution; for a material and irreparable breach the trial is no later than the third day after filing and restitution is ordered 12 to 24 hours later. (A.R.S. 33-1377; source)
  • Trial postponement for good cause is at most three days in justice court or five days in superior court (indicating justice court and superior court hear these actions). (A.R.S. 33-1377; source)
Selling in Arizona?
We buy Arizona houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Which Arizona eviction notice applies to which problem?

The notice an Arizona landlord must send depends on the reason: unpaid rent, a lease breach, a health and safety breach, an irreparable breach, or an end to a periodic tenancy. The statute sets a different number of days for each, and using the wrong one can sink the case.

SituationNotice periodStatute
Unpaid rent5 days after written noticeA.R.S. 33-1368(B)
Material lease breachEnds no sooner than 10 days after receipt if not fixed in 10 daysA.R.S. 33-1368(A)
Health and safety breach under 33-1341Ends no sooner than 5 days after receipt if not fixed in 5 daysA.R.S. 33-1368(A)
Material and irreparable breachImmediate termination noticeA.R.S. 33-1368(A)
Month-to-month tenancy30 days before the rental dateA.R.S. 33-1375(B)
Week-to-week tenancy10 days before the termination dateA.R.S. 33-1375(A)

Under A.R.S. 33-1368, the word days in that section means calendar days, so weekends count.

What must a five-day nonpayment notice say?

It must be written, state that rent is unpaid, and say the landlord intends to terminate the rental agreement if the rent is not paid within five days. That is the statutory wording in 33-1368(B).

The Arizona courts' own information sheet adds that the landlord cannot file the eviction action until after the final day of the notice. It also says that if the tenant did not receive a proper termination notice and a chance to pay the rent and late fees, or if the notice was not properly served, the court must dismiss the action.

Arizona law does not require a specific form. A.R.S. 12-1175(D) says a state agency or an individual court may not adopt or enforce a rule requiring a mandatory or technical form for notices or pleadings in these actions, as long as the notice meets the statutory content requirements.

How is an eviction notice delivered and when is it received?

A notice to a tenant is received when it is delivered in hand or mailed by registered or certified mail to the place the tenant designates, or to the last known residence if none is designated. A.R.S. 33-1313 sets this out.

For mailed notices the statute adds that the tenant is deemed to have received it on the day it is actually received or five days after mailing, whichever comes first. That matters because the 5-day and 10-day periods in 33-1368 count from receipt of the notice, so mailing adds time.

Landlords who want a clean record usually deliver in hand and keep proof, or use certified mail and keep the receipt.

What changes with a ten-day or five-day lease breach notice?

With these notices the tenant gets a chance to fix the problem, and if it is fixed in time the lease does not end. The 10-day notice must specify the acts and omissions that make up the breach and state that the agreement ends on a date not less than ten days after receipt if the breach is not remedied in ten days.

A few details from the statute:

  • Material falsification on the rental application can count as a breach, for example untrue information about occupants, pets, income or employment.
  • Falsification about criminal records, prior evictions or current criminal activity is not curable under that section.
  • The five-day health and safety notice must be fixed within five days, and if the breach is remediable by repair or payment of damages and the tenant fixes it before the date in the notice, the agreement does not end.
  • If the same or a similar health and safety problem recurs during the lease after a cure, the landlord may file a special detainer action ten days after delivering written notice of the second noncompliance.

When can a landlord use an immediate termination notice?

A landlord may serve a notice for immediate termination only for a breach that is both material and irreparable and that occurs on the premises. The statute gives examples and says the list is not exhaustive.

  • Illegal discharge of a weapon
  • Homicide, prostitution, or criminal street gang activity
  • Unlawful manufacturing, selling, using or storing of a controlled substance
  • Threatening or intimidating, or assault
  • Acts found to constitute a nuisance, or breaches that jeopardize the health, safety and welfare of the landlord, agent or another tenant, or involve imminent or actual serious property damage

Once the court case is filed under A.R.S. 33-1377, the trial date and return date must be set no later than the third day after filing. If the court finds the breach occurred by a preponderance of the evidence, it must order restitution not less than 12 nor more than 24 hours later.

How do you end a month-to-month tenancy to sell the house?

A month-to-month tenancy ends with written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date given in the notice. The landlord or the tenant may give it. A week-to-week tenancy needs a written notice at least ten days before the date it ends.

If the tenant stays after the term ends or after termination without the landlord's consent, the landlord may bring an action for possession. When the holdover is willful and not in good faith, the landlord may also recover up to two months of periodic rent or twice the actual damages, whichever is greater.

A landlord who consents in writing to the tenant's continued stay changes the analysis, so any arrangement for a tenant to remain after a sale should be in writing.

How can accepting rent weaken an eviction notice?

Accepting rent after a default can waive the right to terminate for that breach. A.R.S. 33-1371 says that, with the listed exceptions, acceptance of rent or any part of it with knowledge of a default constitutes a waiver of the right to terminate for that breach.

A landlord is not required to accept a partial payment. A landlord who does accept one keeps the right to proceed only if the tenant agrees in a contemporaneous writing to the terms, and that writing must contain a date on which the balance is due. A housing assistance payment is treated differently: accepting it is not accepting a partial payment and does not waive termination.

What notice is needed before the landlord enters to show the house?

The landlord must give at least two days' notice of intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times, except in an emergency or when notice is impracticable. This is in A.R.S. 33-1343.

The same statute says the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent for the landlord to enter to exhibit the unit to prospective or actual purchasers. The landlord cannot abuse access or use it to harass the tenant, and has no other right of entry except by court order, abandonment rules, or surrender of the premises.

What cannot be the reason for an eviction notice?

A landlord may not retaliate by raising rent, cutting services or threatening an action for possession because the tenant made certain complaints. A.R.S. 33-1381 lists complaints to a housing or building code agency about a health and safety violation, complaints to the landlord under 33-1324, and joining a tenants' union.

A complaint within six months before the alleged retaliation creates a presumption that the landlord was retaliating. The landlord can still bring an action if the tenant is in default in rent or if the code violation was caused primarily by the tenant's lack of reasonable care.

More questions about Arizona Eviction Notice Rules

How many days is an eviction notice in Arizona?

It depends on the reason: five days for unpaid rent after written notice, ten days for a curable lease breach, five days for a health and safety breach, and an immediate notice for a material and irreparable breach. A month-to-month tenancy needs 30 days.

Do weekends count toward the five-day notice?

Yes. A.R.S. 33-1368 says that for that section days means calendar days.

Can a landlord evict without a written notice?

For nonpayment and lease breaches the statute calls for written notice. The Arizona courts say the case must be dismissed if the tenant was not given a proper notice and a chance to pay.

Does a landlord have to use a particular form?

No. A.R.S. 12-1175(D) bars courts and state agencies from requiring a mandatory or technical form, as long as the notice meets the statutory content requirements.

Can a landlord show the house to buyers while it is tenant-occupied?

Yes, with at least two days' notice at reasonable times, and the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent. Emergencies and impracticable situations are excepted.
